thread.title_full: Forsyth Army officer killed in WWII identified after 80 years - NewsBreak

author: Dave DeMille
title: Forsyth Army officer killed in WWII identified after 80 years - NewsBreak
text:
By Dave DeMille ,
1 days ago U.S. Army 1st Lt. Robert P. Aikman, a Missouri native killed during World War II, has been formally accounted for more than eight decades after his death, according to a community announcement from the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency .
Aikman, 40, of Forsyth, Missouri, was declared accounted for April 2, 2025, following forensic analysis of remains recovered from a mass grave in what is now Taiwan. His family recently received a full briefing on the identification, allowing additional details to be publicly released.
Aikman served with Battery D, 1st Battalion, 59th Coastal Artillery Corps and was captured during the Japanese invasion of the Philippines in 1942. He remained a prisoner of war until 1944, when Japanese forces attempted to transport Allied POWs to Japan aboard the transport ship Oryoku Maru.
Unaware that POWs were onboard, U.S. carrier-based aircraft attacked the vessel, which later sank in Subic Bay. After multiple land and sea transfers, Aikman was transported aboard another ship, the Enoura Maru, to Takao, Formosa — now known as Kaohsiung, Taiwan.
Japanese records reported that Aikman died Jan. 9, 1945, when U.S. forces sank the Enoura Maru. He was officially declared non-recoverable on Aug. 31, 1949.
Recovery and identification
Following World War II, the American Graves Registration Command searched for missing U.S. service members. In May 1946, recovery teams exhumed a mass grave at Takao containing the remains of 391 individuals. Due to severe commingling, the remains could not be identified and were buried as Unknowns in Honolulu.
Between October 2022 and July 2023, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency disinterred remains associated with the Enoura Maru for renewed analysis. Scientists used dental and anthropological evidence, circumstantial data, and multiple forms of DNA testing — including mitochondrial, nuclear and autosomal DNA — to identify Aikman’s remains.
Aikman’s name appears on the Walls of the Missing at the Manila American Cemetery in the Philippines. A rosette will be placed next to his name to indicate he has been accounted for.
Burial planned in hometown Aikman was scheduled to be buried May 22, 2026, in Forsyth.
More information about the Defense Department’s mission to account for missing service members is available at the DPAA website at dpaa.mil or on social media at facebook.com/dodpaa , linkedin.com/company/dodpaa , instagram.com/dodpaa , or x.com/dodpaa .
This story was created by Dave DeMille, ddemille@gannett.com , with the assistance of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Journalists were involved in every step of the information gathering, review, editing and publishing process. Learn more at cm.usatoday.com/ethical-conduct .
